chapter: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers
title: Living in Europe, counting the money, and the Messengers' warm first reception
summary: Golson now spends half the year in Europe, advises learning the money first, and recalls fans at the Paris station who were really waiting for Maria Callas.

blocks.x: Now you spend half of your life – half your time – half the year there.
Oh, I’ve been there so much. I know the streets and people.

Duke Ellington is famous – I guess we get it through Ben Webster and maybe through Quincy Jones – as a jazz musician, the thing that you can do is, when you go to another culture, eat their food, learn some of their words and their language.
Right. You’re not going to learn much Hungarian – and that will serve you well. Did I . . . ?

Learn how to count the money. The food, yeah. Count the money. The very first thing for me, when you’re in the airport, find out what the money – count the money, because you’ve got to get in a cab or something. Then you go to the restaurant. The food. Then you pick up the other things.
Obviously they treated you well there, because you now spend half the time there – half the year there.

Yeah. They treated us particularly well. Being the first trip there, and Art Blakey being such a recording star – they’d only heard him on the records – open arms, man. Every concert was a success. Just the five of us. It was a success. They loved it. But I’ll tell you what happened. We went – the first time we went to Paris, we came in the train station, and we saw these people coming up with the cameras ready to record. We started doing that, and they ran right past us. Maria Callas was getting off the train in the next car. We thought they were coming for us.
